title: A two-sided tail-dense enumeration in Cantor space
statement:
Work in the universes of [def-weil-size-convention]. Give $V=\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}$ its product topology, each factor being discrete, and its lexicographic order. Let
$$c(x)=\sum_{n\ge0}2x_n3^{-n-1},\qquad D=\{w(01)^\infty:w\text{ a finite binary word}\},\qquad A=V\setminus D.$$
Then $V$ is nonempty, compact Hausdorff, totally disconnected (every connected subset has at most one point), and metrizable. The map $c:V\to[0,1]$ is continuous, injective, and strictly order preserving. The set $D$ is countably infinite, none of its points is eventually constant, and every nonempty basic cylinder specified by a finite initial word contains infinitely many points of $D$. There exists a bijection $v:\mathbb N\to D$; for any such enumeration, every nonempty open $B\subseteq V$ and every $N\in\mathbb N$ admit $k\ge N$ with $v_k\in B$. The set $A$ is dense in $V$. For each $d\in D$ there are sequences $(x_m^-),(x_m^+)$ in $A$ converging to $d$ such that $c(x_m^-)<c(d)<c(x_m^+)$ for every $m$.

proof.text: For a binary word $w$ of length $r$, put $[w]=\{x:x_i=w_i\ (i<r)\}$. These cylinders form a basis: a finite list of coordinate conditions is refined at any of its points by fixing the initial segment through its largest coordinate. Each cylinder is open and closed, since its complement is the union of the other finitely many length-$r$ cylinders. The all-zero sequence makes $V$ nonempty. Two different points differ in a coordinate, whose two disjoint clopen fibres separate them; hence $V$ is Hausdorff. A connected subset containing both points would be separated by those fibres, so every connected subset has at most one point.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Binary product topology and coordinate separation.

proof.text: Every binary factor is compact: from any open cover choose an open containing $0$ and one containing $1$. Apply [lem-weil-pbc-tychonoff-product-quasi-compact] (products of quasi-compact spaces, i.e. spaces in which every open cover has a finite subcover, are quasi-compact) to get compactness of $V$. For metrizability apply [lem-sfb-compact-countable-separating-metrizable] with $X=V$, $Y_n=\{0,1\}$ with its discrete metric, and $u_n(x)=x_n$. The projections are continuous by the product topology and separate distinct sequences. All hypotheses of that node, including compactness of $X$, now hold.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Compactness and metrizability of Cantor space.

proof.text: For $x\in V$ set $a_i=2x_i\in\{0,1,2\}$. The coordinate map $x\mapsto a$ is continuous: the inverse image of any finite-coordinate cylinder is open. Apply [lem-sfb-real-positional-digit-expansion] with $b=3$. Its series is exactly $c(x)$, is convergent, has values in $[0,1]$, and depends continuously on $x$. A map into $[0,1]$ is continuous when its composition with inclusion into $\mathbb R$ is continuous, directly by the subspace topology. The same node supplies the prefix-tail formula and bounds for all ternary digit sequences.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Definition and continuity of the ternary coordinate.

proof.text: If $x<y$ lexicographically, let $j$ be their first unequal coordinate, so $x_j=0$, $y_j=1$. Split both series after $j+1$ terms using [lem-sfb-real-positional-digit-expansion]. Writing $X=F_3((2x_{j+1+i})_i)$ and $Y=F_3((2y_{j+1+i})_i)$ gives $$c(y)-c(x)=3^{-j-1}(2+Y-X)\geq3^{-j-1}>0,$$ since $0\leq X,Y\leq1$. Thus $c$ is strictly order preserving. Any two distinct binary sequences have a first unequal coordinate, and one is lexicographically smaller; consequently $c$ is injective.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. First-unequal-digit calculation.

proof.text: Finite binary words are countable: encode a length-$r$ word $w$ by $2^r+\sum_{i<r}w_i2^i$, lying in $[2^r,2^{r+1})$. The interval recovers $r$, and successive remainders modulo $2$ recover the digits. To each $d\in D$ assign the least code of a word $w$ with $d=w(01)^\infty$. Equal codes give equal words and hence equal $d$, so this is an injection $D\to\mathbb N$. Every $d\in D$ contains infinitely many $0$s and $1$s in its alternating tail, and is therefore not eventually constant.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Countability and non-endpoint property of the prescribed set.

proof.text: Fix a word $w$. For each $r\geq0$ the sequence $d_r=w0^r1(01)^\infty$ belongs to $[w]\cap D$. These sequences are distinct: if $r<s$, their digits at position $|w|+r$ are $1$ and $0$ respectively. Thus every cylinder contains infinitely many points of $D$. In particular, using the empty word shows $D$ is infinite.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. An explicit infinite family in every cylinder.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-countable-infinite-bijection] to $\mathbb N$ and the countable infinite set $D$ obtained above, yielding a bijection $v:\mathbb N\to D$. For any such $v$, any nonempty open $B$, and any $N$, choose a cylinder $[w]\subseteq B$ through one point of $B$. The infinite set $D\cap[w]$ cannot be contained in the finite set $\{v_0,\ldots,v_{N-1}\}$. Choose $d$ outside that finite set and use surjectivity to write $d=v_k$; injectivity then forces $k\geq N$. This proves tail density for every bijective enumeration, including $N=0$.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Existence of an enumeration and the elementary finite-exclusion argument.

proof.text: Every cylinder $[w]$ contains $w0^\infty$. This sequence is eventually constant, whereas no member of $D$ is; hence it belongs to $A$. Every nonempty open contains a cylinder, so meets $A$, which proves that $A$ is dense.

source.place: Paragraph (3), agent-formulated pure-topology auxiliary below the countably split profinite cover; the blueprint supplies context, not this topology theorem. Dense complement by eventually zero sequences.

proof.text: Fix $d\in D$. For each $m\geq0$, choose indices $p_m,q_m\geq m$ with $d_{p_m}=1$, $d_{q_m}=0$; they exist because the alternating tail has both digits arbitrarily far out. Define $x_m^-$ to agree with $d$ below $p_m$, to have digit $0$ at $p_m$, and to be constantly $0$ thereafter. Define $x_m^+$ to agree below $q_m$, have digit $1$ at $q_m$, and be constantly $0$ thereafter. Both are eventually zero and thus in $A$. Their first unequal digits with $d$ give $x_m^-<d<x_m^+$, so Step 4 gives $c(x_m^-)<c(d)<c(x_m^+)$. For each fixed prefix length $r$, all $m\geq r$ make both sequences agree with $d$ on that prefix. By the cylinder basis this is exactly convergence to $d$ in $V$.
